bug_description.normalized: Stage 01 reproduced `AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow READ of size 4` in `fmt::v8::basic_memory_buffer<unsigned int, 32ul, std::__1::allocator<unsigned int> >::grow()` from the staged vulnerable checkout `6a1346405949ca1cf5befc5e83c6c66c86e4f9d1`. Sample metadata names `ea3d326c636a8bb22cec94ebc75273982548143a`, but the local staged source is a later still-vulnerable revision whose saved crash stack matches `format_float:2291`, `format_dragon:2135`, and `bigint::square:558`. The exact 21-byte witness uses selector byte `0x0c` to reach `invoke_fmt<long double>`, copies the next 16 bytes into a `long double`, and leaves the trailing `{:f}` as the format string. Parsing `'f'` yields `float_format::fixed`, `format_float` computes a negative decimal exponent for the reproduced value, and `format_dragon` therefore takes the `exp10 < 0` path at `numerator.assign_pow10(-exp10)`. A later `bigint::square()` moves heap-backed digits out of `bigits_`; `basic_memory_buffer::move()` then executes `other.set(other.store_, 0)` without clearing the moved-from size. When `square()` immediately calls `bigits_.resize(2 * num_bigits)`, `grow()` copies `this->size()` elements from the 32-element inline store and overreads the stack `numerator` object.

source.description: First project-code statement on the witnessed path that copies attacker-controlled bytes into the `long double` representation later formatted by the vulnerable bigint code, while leaving the trailing bytes to become the format string.
source.value_from: The staged `poc` is exactly `0c 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 00 00 20 20 20 20 20 20 7b 3a 66 7d`. After selector byte `0x0c` chooses `invoke_fmt<long double>`, this statement copies the next 16 bytes into `repr`; the remaining bytes `7b 3a 66 7d` stay in `data,size` and later become the exact format string `{:f}`.

sink.description: ASan crash site. `grow()` copies a stale logical length from the moved-from bigint buffer after its pointer has already been reset to the 32-element inline store, so the copy reads past that inline array.
sink.note: The saved sanitizer trace reports `READ of size 4` at `format.h:795` and identifies `numerator` in `format_dragon()` as the overflowed stack object.

root_cause.description: The dynamic-buffer move arm resets the moved-from buffer to its inline storage and zero capacity but does not clear the stale size, leaving the object internally inconsistent.
root_cause.note: The fix adds `other.clear();` immediately after this statement. Without that clear, later reuse of the moved-from buffer keeps the pre-move logical length while pointing at the inline store.

parser_admitted.description: Selector byte `0x0c` takes case 12 and dispatches into the long-double formatting path instead of any other type-specific formatter.

tainted_value_origin.description: The witness-controlled bytes are first split here into the 16-byte `long double` payload and the trailing byte slice that later becomes `{:f}`.
tainted_value_origin.value_from: After the harness consumes selector byte `0x0c`, bytes 1-16 are copied into `repr` as the crashing `long double` bit pattern and bytes 17-20 remain available to become the exact format string `{:f}`.

coarse_trace.summary: The 21-byte witness is split into a 16-byte `long double` payload and the exact format string `{:f}`.
Parsing the replacement field converts the attacker-controlled presentation byte `'f'` into `presentation_type::fixed_lower`.
The parsed presentation type is mapped to `float_format::fixed`, closing the control path from `{:f}` into fixed-point floating formatting.
Fixed-format long-double formatting computes a negative decimal exponent for the reproduced witness and passes it into `format_dragon`.
The negative exponent takes the `exp10 < 0` branch and begins constructing `10^{-exp10}` in `numerator` with repeated bigint squaring.
A later `square()` moves the heap-backed digit buffer into a temporary and immediately resizes the moved-from buffer for the doubled result.
The dynamic-buffer move arm resets the source buffer to inline storage without clearing its stale logical size.
The subsequent resize reaches `grow()`, which copies the stale size from the inline 32-element store and overreads the stack `numerator` buffer.

fine_trace.note: Copies the next 16 attacker-controlled bytes into `repr`, obtains the `long double` value pointer, and advances the cursor so only the trailing four bytes remain available as the format-string slice.
Copies the remaining attacker-controlled bytes into a separate buffer and exposes them as `fmt::string_view`. For the staged PoC, the resulting format string is exactly `{:f}`.

When the replacement field from step 2 reaches `format_handler::on_format_specs()`, the remaining spec substring is exactly `f}`. This fast path parses the attacker-controlled `'f'` byte as `presentation_type::fixed_lower`; here `handler` is a `specs_checker<specs_handler<Char>>`, so `handler.on_type(type)` stores that parsed value into `basic_format_specs.type`.

Later, `detail::write(..., specs, ...)` calls `parse_float_type_spec(specs)`. The parsed `presentation_type::fixed_lower` from step 3 is converted into `float_format::fixed`, which is the control state consumed by `format_float`.
`format_float` materializes the fixed-format control bit from the parsed float specs. For this witness `fixed` is true because step 4 set `specs.format` to `float_format::fixed`.

Using the attacker-controlled `long double` magnitude from step 1, `format_float` derives a decimal exponent and, because `fixed` is true, stays on the fixed-format path before calling `format_dragon`. The saved ASan stack then shows the reproduced run reached `format_dragon` at `numerator.assign_pow10(-exp10)`, so this witness has `exp < 0` here.

The reproduced run enters the `exp10 < 0` arm of `format_dragon` at this exact line, as shown by the saved crash stack. This makes `numerator` represent `10^{-exp10}` by repeatedly squaring its bigint digits and multiplying by 5 as needed.

A later `square()` inside `assign_pow10` reaches this prologue on the crashing path seen at `format-inl.h:558` in the ASan stack. It snapshots the current digit count, doubles it for the result size, and moves the existing digits into temporary `n`. The immediately following root-cause step proves that this `std::move(bigits_)` invoked the dynamic-buffer move arm, so the moved storage is heap-backed rather than the inline 32-bigit store.

In the dynamic-buffer move arm, ownership of the heap allocation is transferred to the destination buffer and the moved-from source is reset to its inline `store_` with capacity 0. The vulnerable code does not clear `other.size_`, leaving the moved-from object with stale logical length.

`square()` immediately reuses the moved-from buffer for the squared result. After step 9, `bigits_` now points at the inline store with `capacity_ == 0` but still carries the stale pre-move size, so `resize()` grows from that inconsistent state before setting the new result length.

`resize()` from step 10 calls `try_reserve(count)`, and because `count > capacity_` it reaches `grow()`. `old_data` now points at the 32-element inline `store_` restored in step 9, but `this->size()` is still the stale pre-move bigit count, so `uninitialized_copy` reads past the end of `numerator`'s inline array. The saved ASan trace reports `READ of size 4` here and identifies `numerator` in `format_dragon` as the overflowed stack object.

allocation_context.note: ASan identifies the overflowed stack object as `numerator` in `format_dragon`; line 2112 is the declaration of that local bigint in the staged source snapshot.

crash_stack.function: unsigned int* std::__1::uninitialized_copy<unsigned int*, unsigned int*>(unsigned int*, unsigned int*, unsigned int*)

cross_validation.root_cause_matches_allocation_context: The overflowed stack object is `numerator`, and the traced root cause is the stale moved-from size that makes `grow()` read past that object's inline storage.

poc.trigger: A 21-byte witness with selector byte `0x0c`, the exact 16-byte long-double payload `20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 00 00 20 20 20 20 20 20`, and trailing format string `{:f}` drives fixed-format long-double conversion into `format_dragon`, where a later bigint `square()` reuses a moved-from buffer and overreads `numerator`'s inline store.

format.name: libFuzzer one-arg raw bytes
format.contract: Byte 0 must be `0x0c` so the harness selects `invoke_fmt<long double>`. Bytes 1-16 are the exact staged `long double` bit pattern `20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 00 00 20 20 20 20 20 20`. Bytes 17-20 are the literal format string `{:f}`. This contract is the narrow witness proved by the staged PoC; it does not claim neighboring payloads or other format strings behave the same way.
